[[File:Glaucium flavum MHNT.BOT.2007.40.129.jpg|thumb]]

'''''Glaucium flavum''''', the '''yellow horned poppy''',<ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=42}}</ref> '''yellow hornpoppy''' or '''sea poppy''', is a summer [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Papaveraceae]]. It is native to Europe, Northern Africa, [[Macaronesia]] and temperate zones in Western Asia. The plant grows on the seashore and is never found inland. All parts of the plant, including the seeds, are [[toxic]]. It is classed as a [[noxious weed]] in some areas of North America, where it is an [[introduced species]]. It is grown in gardens as a short-lived perennial but usually grown as a [[biennial plant|biennial]].

==Description==
It has thick, leathery deeply segmented, wavy, bluish-grey leaves, which are coated in a layer of water-retaining wax. The sepal, petals and stamen have a similar structure and form to the [[Papaver rhoeas|red poppy (''Papaver rhoeas'')]], except the sepals are not hairy.<ref name=Brimble>{{Cite book|title=Flowers in Britain|page=54|author = L. J. F. Brimble|year=1947|publisher=Macmillan and Co|location=London}}</ref> It grows up to {{convert|30|-|90|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=31 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}}</ref> on branched, grey stems. It blooms in summer,<ref name="rhs">{{cite web|title=Glaucium flavum|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8033/Glaucium-flavum/Details|publisher=rhs.org.uk|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref> between June and October.<ref name=Readers /><ref name="norfolk">{{cite web|title=Yellow horned-poppy Glucium flavum|url=https://www.norfolkwildlifetrust.org.uk/wildlife-in-norfolk/species-explorer/plants/yellow-horned-poppy|publisher=norfolkwildlifetrust.org.uk|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref> It has bright yellow or orange flowers,<ref name="rhs" /> that are {{convert|7.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} across.<ref name=Readers /> Later, it produces a very long, upright,<ref name="rhs" /> thin,<ref name=Readers /> distinctive horn shaped capsule, which is {{convert|15|-|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} long. It is divided into two chambers,<ref name=Brimble /> which split open to reveal the seeds.<ref name=Readers />

==Taxonomy==
It was first published and described by [[Heinrich Johann Nepomuk von Crantz]] in 'Stirp. Austr. Fasc.' (Stirpium Austriarum) vol.2 on page 133 in 1763.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Kurzböck| last = Crantz| first = Heinrich Johann Nepomuk| title = Stirpium Austriarum Fasciculus II| location = Viennæ Austriæ| date = 1763| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IhoBNGCUEA4C}}</ref><ref name="plantlist">{{cite web|title=Glaucium flavum Crantz is an accepted name|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2826358|date=23 March 2012|publisher=theplantlist.org|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Papaveraceae Glaucium flavum Crantz|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=161798-3|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref> The species [[epithet]] ''flavum'' is Latin for yellow and indicates its flower colour.<ref>Archibald William Smith {{google books|ahNMkgoNJ7IC|A Gardener's Handbook of Plant Names: Their Meanings and Origins|page=258}}</ref>

It is commonly known as ''sea-poppy'',<ref name=Fernie>W. T. Fernie {{google books|2g8lBQAAQBAJ|Herbal Simples: Approved for Modern Uses of Cure (1897)|page=441}}</ref> ''horned-poppy'', and ''yellow horned-poppy''.<ref name="rhs"/><ref name="grin">{{cite web|title=Taxon: Glaucium flavum Crantz|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=17621|publisher=ars-grin.gov|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref>

''G. flavum'' was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 25 May 1995, then updated on 9 May 2011,<ref name="grin" /> and is an accepted name by the [[Royal Horticultural Society]].<ref name="rhs" />

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant|native]] to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of Western Asia.<ref name="grin" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Hassler|first1=M.|title=Accepted scientific name: Glaucium flavum Crantz (accepted name)|url=http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/df52718273f03dd4307bd7a905b10d9b|date=September 2017|publisher=catalogueoflife.org|access-date=2 November 2017|archive-date=26 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190826080523/http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/df52718273f03dd4307bd7a905b10d9b|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Range===
[[File:Glaucium flavum 1.JPG|thumb|Growing in sand in Spain]]
It is found in North Africa, within [[Macaronesia]], [[Canary Islands]], [[Algeria]], [[Libya]], [[Tunisia]] and [[Morocco]]. Within Western Asia it is found in the Caucasus, [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], [[Cyprus]], [[Egypt]] (in the [[Sinai Peninsula|Sinai]]), [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]] and [[Turkey]]. In eastern Europe, it is found within [[Ukraine]]. In middle Europe, it is in [[Belgium]], [[Germany]], [[Netherlands]] and [[Slovakia]]. In northern Europe, in [[Denmark]], [[Ireland]], [[Norway]], [[Sweden]] and [[United Kingdom]]. In south-eastern Europe, within [[Albania]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Croatia]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]], [[Montenegro]], [[Sicily]] and [[Malta]], [[North Macedonia]], [[Romania]], and [[Slovenia]]. In southwestern Europe, it is found in [[France]], [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]].<ref name="grin" /><ref name=Cambrolle>{{cite journal |last1=Cambrollé |first1=Jesús |last2=Redondo-Gómez |first2=Susana |last3=Mateos-Naranjo |first3=Enrique |last4=Luque |first4=Teresa |last5=Figueroa |first5=Manuel Enrique |title=Physiological responses to salinity in the yellow-horned poppy, ''Glaucium flavum'' |journal=Plant Physiol Biochem. |date=February 2011 |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=186–94|doi=10.1016/j.plaphy.2010.11.008 |pmid=21168338 }}</ref>

===Habitat===
It grows in coastal habitats on shingle banks and beaches,<ref name="norfolk" /><ref name=Cambrolle/> but can also be found on cliff tops and in sand dunes.<ref name=Readers />

==Toxicity==
It produces an orange foul-smelling sap, if cut open.<ref name=Readers /> All parts of the plant, including the seeds, are toxic, and can cause a wide range of symptoms if eaten,<ref name=Readers /> and [[respiratory failure]], resulting in death.<ref>Cooper, M. R. & A. W. Johnson. 1998. Poisonous plants and fungi in Britain: animal and human poisoning. (Cooper & Johnson ed.2)</ref>

==Culture==
It is referenced in various poems.
<poem>
A poppy grows upon the shore,
   Bursts her twin cups in summer late:
Her leaves are glaucus-green and hoar,
   Her petals yellow, delicate.

She has no lovers like the red,
   That dances with the noble corn:
Her blossoms on the waves are shed,
   Where she stands shivering and forlorn.
</poem>
::::''Shorter Poems'' [[Robert Bridges]].<ref>{{cite web|title=The shorter poems of Robert Bridges (1890)|url=https://archive.org/stream/poemsofroshorter00bridrich/poemsofroshorter00bridrich_djvu.txt|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref>

Sea Poppies:
<poem>
Amber husk
fluted with gold,
fruit on the sand
marked with a rich grain,

treasure
spilled near the shrub-pines
to bleach on the boulders:

your stalk has caught root
among wet pebbles
and drift flung by the sea
and grated shells
and split conch-shells.

Beautiful, widespread,
fire upon leaf,
what meadow yields
so fragrant a leaf
as your bright leaf?
</poem>
[[H.D.]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Sea Poppies|url=https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48187/sea-poppies|publisher=poetryfoundation.org|access-date=2 November 2017}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[Glaucine]] is the main [[alkaloid]] component in ''Glaucium flavum''.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=G.B. Lapa |author2=O.P. Sheichenko |author3=A.G. Serezhechkin |author4=O.N. Tolkachev |date=August 2004 |title=HPLC Determination of Glaucine in Yellow Horn Poppy Grass (''Glaucium flavum Crantz'') |journal=Pharmaceutical Chemistry Journal |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=441–442 |issn=0091-150X |doi=10.1023/B:PHAC.0000048907.58847.c6 |s2cid=44040818 |quote=S-(+)-Glaucine (C<sub>21</sub>H<sub>25</sub>NO<sub>4</sub>) is the main alkaloid component in the grass of yellow horn poppy (''Glaucium luteum L.'', syn. ''Glaucium flavum Crantz'') of the family Papaveraceae}}</ref> [[Glaucine]] has [[bronchodilator]] and [[antiinflammatory]] effects, acting as a [[Phosphodiesterase inhibitor|PDE<sub>4</sub> inhibitor]] and [[calcium channel blocker]],<ref>{{cite journal | author = Cortijo J, Villagrasa V, Pons R, Berto L, Martí-Cabrera M, Martinez-Losa M, Domenech T, Beleta J, Morcillo EJ | date = Aug 1999 | title = Bronchodilator and anti-inflammatory activities of glaucine: In vitro studies in human airway smooth muscle and polymorphonuclear leukocytes | journal = [[British Journal of Pharmacology]] | volume = 127 | issue = 7| pages = 1641–51 | pmid = 10455321 | doi = 10.1038/sj.bjp.0702702 | pmc = 1566148 }}</ref> and is used medically as an [[antitussive]] in some countries.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Rühle KH, Criscuolo D, Dieterich HA, Köhler D, Riedel G | date = May 1984 | title = Objective evaluation of dextromethorphan and glaucine as antitussive agents | journal = British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology | volume = 17 | issue = 5| pages = 521–4 | pmid = 6375709 | pmc = 1463443 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2125.1984.tb02384.x }}</ref> Glaucine may produce side effects such as [[sedation]], [[fatigue (medical)|fatigue]], and a [[hallucinogen]]ic effect characterised by colourful visual images,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Rovinskiĭ VI | date = Sep 1989 | title = A case of hallucinogen-like action of glaucine. (Russian) | journal = Klinicheskaia Meditsina (Mosk) | volume = 67 | issue = 9| pages = 107–8 | pmid = 2586025 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Rovinskiĭ VI | year = 2006 | title = Acute glaucine syndrome in the physician's practice: the clinical picture and potential danger. (Russian) | journal = Klinicheskaia Meditsina (Mosk) | volume = 84 | issue = 11| pages = 68–70 | pmid = 17243616 }}</ref> and as a [[recreational drug]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Dargan PI, Button J, Hawkins L, Archer JR, Ovaska H, Lidder S, Ramsey J, Holt DW, Wood DM | date = May 2008 | title = Detection of the pharmaceutical agent glaucine as a recreational drug | journal = European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology | volume = 64 | issue = 5| pages = 553–4 | pmid = 18204834 | doi = 10.1007/s00228-007-0451-9 | s2cid = 21348503 }}</ref>
For a detailed bibliography on glaucine and ''Glaucium flavum'' see: [[National Agricultural Library]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nal.usda.gov/agricola?DB=local&CNT=25&Search_Arg=Glaucium+flavum&Search_Code=GKEY&STARTDB=AGRIDB|title=NAL Catalog (AGRICOLA): Titles|website=agricola.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>

In the past, it was known in [[Hampshire]], UK, as 'squatmore', and the roots were used to treat [[bruises]],<ref name="Readers" /> and pains in the breast, stomach and [[intestines]].<ref name=Fernie />
